claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation in FCC/BCC HEA multilayers under sustained loading is governed by dislocation–twin interactions.
Compositional complexity influences dislocation–twin interactions in HEA multilayers.
Severe lattice distortion influences dislocation–twin interactions in HEA multilayers.
The starting material is an undeformed nanoscale multilayer coating containing FCC and BCC phases.
The proposed intervention is sustained loading at 500 MPa.
The proposed test is conducted at room temperature.
The proposed test uses a strain rate of 10^-4 s^-1.
Plastic deformation proceeds through dislocation nucleation and glide.
Plastic deformation involves deformation-twin formation and growth.
Loading will produce a 20% increase in plastic strain relative to the starting baseline.
The undeformed baseline has zero plastic strain.
The hypothesis is bounded to a maximum strain of 10%.
The exact effects of compositional complexity and lattice distortion on dislocation–twin interactions are not well understood.
The proposed falsification experiment is a uniaxial tensile test with in situ characterization.
The experiment will measure the stress–strain curve, dislocation density, and twin fraction.
The hypothesis is falsified if plastic strain is less than 10% after 10% applied strain.

contradictions.description: A percentage increase relative to a zero-plastic-strain baseline is mathematically undefined; interpreted literally, a 20% increase over zero remains zero and does not express progressive plastic deformation.

The intervention is described as sustained loading at a fixed stress, whereas the prescribed strain rate and tensile test imply strain-controlled ramp loading. The loading protocol is therefore not consistently defined.

The falsification threshold of 10% plastic strain does not directly negate the predicted 20% relative increase, especially because that relative increase is referenced to zero. Thus the rule does not decisively test the stated quantitative prediction.
